The story is told almost entirely from a close third-person perspective aligned with Dr. Ruth Amsel and the collective experience of the linguistics faculty. While there are characters who represent the frustrating and bureaucratic institution—such as Ms. Diane Farrow from facilities or the negligent contractors—the narrative does not dive into their mindsets, motivations, or beliefs. Instead, they are observed strictly from the outside through the lens of the faculty's dry, ironic detachment, and there are no truly morally ambiguous or repugnant viewpoints explored in depth.
